Based on the data you provided, the short answer is: **No, it is extremely unlikely that you will be able to see the Moon with the naked eye.**

Here is the breakdown of why, based on the specific astronomical conditions you listed:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Solar Altitude)
The most significant factor is the Sun's position. At an altitude of **68.338 degrees**, the Sun is very high in the sky. This creates intense atmospheric scattering (Rayleigh scattering), which makes the sky "bright daylight." 

For a celestial object to be visible during the day, it generally needs to be very close to the Sun (to be seen as a faint "ghost" disc) or very far from the Sun (where the sky is darker). At **90.942 degrees** away from the Sun, the Moon is in a "middle ground" where the sky is still too bright to provide the necessary contrast.

### 2. Moon Altitude and Phase
The Moon is at a relatively low altitude (**12.202 degrees**). While it is technically above the horizon, it is sitting in a part of the sky where the atmosphere is thicker. This causes more "airmass" to interfere with the light. 

Furthermore, at **50.95% illumination** (a First Quarter phase), the Moon is not a thin crescent. A thin crescent can sometimes be seen during the day because it is physically close to the Sun's glare; a half-moon has a much larger surface area, but it doesn't have the "proximity" advantage to peek through the daylight.

### 3. Contrast Ratios
Human vision relies on contrast. In "bright daylight," the luminance of the sky is orders of magnitude higher than the reflected light of a half-illuminated Moon. Even though the Moon is physically there, the "signal" (the Moon's light) is completely overwhelmed by the "noise" (the Sun's scattered light in the atmosphere).

### The Verdict
If you were to look toward the azimuth of **114.138 degrees** (roughly East-Southeast), you would see a bright, blue-white sky. You would not see a distinct lunar disc. 

**The only way you would see it:**
If you had a pair of **high-powered binoculars or a telescope**, you would likely be able to spot it easily because those tools "crop out" the surrounding bright sky and concentrate the light of the Moon into your pupil. But with unaided eyesight, it will remain invisible.
